newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Extradition studied for Bosnia war suspects-Arbour.
newsitem.headline: Extradition studied for Bosnia war suspects-Arbour.

text.p: The chief prosecutor for the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia said on Tuesday she was studying various options to ensure the extradition of war crimes suspects.

"I'm exploring all options ranging from the mildest to the most severe. I believe it is still worth pursuing discussions with respect to voluntary surrender," Louise Arbour told a news conference in Sarajevo.
The Canadian judge spoke after holding talks with leaders from Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic in her first visit to the Balkans since she took over as prosecutor last year.
Bosnian Serb authorities made clear they would cooperate with the tribunal "except so far as what was termed extradition was concerned", Arbour said.
Bosnian Serb leaders have refused to hand over those indicted by the tribunal, including wartime leader Radovan Karadzic and former army commander Ratko Mladic.

Arbour said she rejected arguments by the Serbs that their laws barred extradition. But she said she suggested they publicly encourage those indicted to turn themselves in as proof of their professed "goodwill" towards the tribunal.
Out of 74 suspects indicted by the U.N. tribunal, only seven are in custody. Critics say there will be no reconciliation among former foes if those indicted are allowed to go free.

The NATO alliance, fearing a backlash against its troops, has ruled out ordering its peacekeeping force to track down war crimes suspects. Some U.S. officials have suggested forming a special international unit that would make the arrests.
Arbour said "a combination of initiatives" would prove the best approach to extradition but declined to go into details.
"The least is said about a particular strategy the more likely the strategy is likely to bear fruit," she said.
Earlier on Tuesday, the lawyer for indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic attended Arbour's meeting with Serb officials in Pale, outside Sarajevo.
Reporters saw Belgrade lawyer Igor Pantelic, who is representing Karadzic, attend the beginning of the meeting.
Karadzic lives in Pale, the government seat of Bosnian Serb territory, and diplomats say he still wields power behind the scenes.
Arbour defended the tribunal's work despite the refusal by former warring factions to hand over suspects, saying she expected all those indicted to be brought to justice eventually.
"It seems to me inconcievable that difficulties that we're presently encountering with respect to arrests should in any way be fatal to the mission of this tribunal."
She added: "Within a time frame that at this point it would be foolish to predict, we will bring to trial the people that we have indicted and many more."
The prosecutor's office was still pursuing investigations and it would be issuing more indictments in the future.
"We still have lots of ongoing investigations and I foresee a very active prosecuting agenda."
Arbour, who held talks with Croatian authorities earlier in her trip, was scheduled to travel to neighbouring Yugoslavia, comprised of Serbia and Montenegro.
